opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most interesting opportunities right now, but it's also one where people can easily get the framing wrong.

When we say RSI—recursive self-improvement—for science, the core idea is that you have a system that doesn't just answer questions, but actually proposes hypotheses, designs experiments, looks at the results, and then improves its own way of doing research. The loop closes. And science is a really natural domain for this, because science already has a built-in verifier: reality. You run the experiment, and the outcome tells you whether you were right. That's very different from, say, open-ended chat, where the reward signal is fuzzy.

From a commercialization perspective, I see a few layers. The first and most immediate is in domains where the feedback loop is fast and cheap—things like code, math, chip design, certain kinds of materials simulation, or optimization problems. There you can iterate thousands of times a day, so the self-improvement actually compounds. Companies that build those loops well can deliver real value quickly, because the output is directly measurable: a faster kernel, a better circuit layout, a proof that checks.

The second layer is wet-lab science—biology, chemistry, drug discovery. The potential payoff is enormous, but the loop is slow and expensive. Each experiment might take days or weeks and cost real money. So the bottleneck isn't really the intelligence of the model; it's the throughput of the physical world. Commercially, I think the winners there will be the ones who combine AI with automation—robotic labs, high-throughput screening—so that they can actually close the loop at a meaningful speed. Owning the data generation pipeline becomes the moat, more than owning the model.

The third point, which I think is underappreciated, is that the business model matters a lot. If you sell RSI-for-science as a tool, a SaaS product, you capture a small fraction of the value. If a system genuinely discovers a new drug candidate or a new material, the value is in the IP, in the discovery itself. So I think we'll see more companies that look less like software vendors and more like research organizations or even biotech companies that happen to be AI-native.

That said, I'd be cautious about the hype. A lot of what's called "AI scientist" today is still closer to a very capable research assistant. It can search literature, write code, run analyses. That's useful, but the hard part of science is often knowing which question to ask, and noticing when something surprising is happening—when the data doesn't fit your mental model. Current systems are still not great at that kind of taste and judgment. And true recursive self-improvement, where the system improves its own research methodology in a sustained way, hasn't really been demonstrated at scale yet.

So my view is: it's a real opportunity, probably one of the biggest, but the near-term money is in narrow domains with good verifiers, and the long-term prize goes to whoever figures out how to make the loop both fast and grounded in reality. The people who understand both the science and the AI deeply will have a big advantage, because you need to know where the model can be trusted and where it can't.

r001.rationale: The response describes automated research loops and says they can compound, but it does not state that automating scientific research improves the training efficiency of large models.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about recursive self-improvement for science, I'd separate two things: the research question of whether a system can genuinely improve its own capabilities, and the commercial question of where that actually creates value today. And honestly, the commercial opportunity is less about "the AI improves itself" and more about closing the loop between hypothesis, experiment, and feedback at a scale and speed humans can't match.

Science is a search problem with an extremely expensive evaluation function. Running a wet-lab experiment, synthesizing a material, or doing a large simulation costs real money and real time. So the first place I see commercial traction is wherever you can make that evaluation cheap or partly automated. Drug discovery, materials, chip design, protein engineering. In those domains, if a model can propose candidates, run a cheap surrogate, learn from the outcome, and refine its own proposal strategy, you've got a flywheel. Each cycle makes the next cycle better. That's the "self-improvement" part, but it's grounded in real-world signal rather than the model just rewriting its own code.

The second piece is what I'd call the infrastructure layer. Someone has to build the orchestration: the agents that design experiments, the verifiers that check results, the data pipelines that feed outcomes back into training. That's a product in itself. Labs don't want to assemble this from scratch, and the companies that provide a reliable loop will have a durable position, because the data that accumulates in that loop is proprietary and compounding.

Now, where I'd be careful. A lot of the hype assumes the model can judge its own progress. In math or code you have verifiers, so self-improvement works fairly cleanly. In open-ended science, the reward signal is noisy and sometimes delayed by years. If you optimize against a weak proxy, you get a system that's very confident and very wrong. So the near-term business is not "autonomous scientist." It's "massively accelerated assistant" where the human still owns the final judgment and the model is learning from each round. That's less glamorous, but it's where I'd put money right now.

And one more thing on timing. The cost of inference is dropping fast, and that changes the economics. Ideas that were unaffordable two years ago, like running ten thousand simulated experiments overnight to narrow down a candidate list, are becoming routine. When that gets cheap enough, the bottleneck shifts entirely to the physical world, and whoever controls the physical experimentation capacity, the robotic labs, the foundries, becomes very valuable. So I'd watch that intersection of AI and automated experimentation closely. That's where RSI for science stops being a research slogan and becomes a business.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes automated experiment-feedback loops that help a model refine proposals and feed outcomes into training, but does not clearly state that increasing scientific research automation improves the training efficiency of large models.

astra-6.text:
I think recursive self-improvement for science is a promising commercialization opportunity because progress can be measured against something concrete. You propose a new material, run a simulation or an experiment, and see whether its properties improve. That feedback can help the system become better at choosing the next experiment.

But the key is closing that loop. A model that generates interesting hypotheses is useful, but someone still has to test them. If experiments take months and cost a lot of money, improving the model alone won’t make the whole process fast. So I would start with a narrow domain where testing is relatively cheap, feedback is reliable, and a better result has clear economic value.

The commercial product could be an integrated research workflow: propose candidates, test them, analyze failures, and use those results to guide the next round. Customers can pay for shorter development cycles or higher success rates without needing to care whether we call it RSI.

There’s also an important distinction here: improving a candidate through repeated experiments is not necessarily improving the research system itself. The bigger opportunity is a system that learns from those experiments and becomes more effective on future problems. Demonstrating that reliably would be a meaningful step.

r001.rationale: The response describes a research system learning from experimental feedback and improving its choices, but it does not state that increasing scientific-research automation improves large-model training efficiency.

sol-6.1.text:
I think recursive self-improvement for science is a very interesting commercialization opportunity because science gives you a way to close the loop. The AI proposes a hypothesis or an experiment, you run it, and the result tells you whether you’re making progress. That feedback can help improve the next proposal.

But the key question is: what exactly is improving? If the system is just generating more candidates, that’s useful, but it’s different from improving its ability to discover things. You need reliable evaluation and a way to turn experimental results into better models, better tools, or better search strategies.

Commercially, I would start with a narrow problem where experiments are relatively fast and the outcome has clear value. You don’t have to solve all of science. If you can help a company reach a useful result with fewer experiments, that’s already a business. The harder part is connecting the AI to the experimental workflow and making sure the feedback is trustworthy. That loop is where I think a lot of the value could be.

r001.rationale: The response describes using experimental feedback to improve future proposals, models, tools, or search strategies, but does not state that automating scientific research improves large-model training efficiency.
